lesson.title: Plurals & i-Mutation
lesson.subtitle: Mann→Männer is man→men: umlaut is English's fossil and German's living tool

hook.title: The Fossil You Speak Daily
hook.content: Say man and men. Foot and feet. Mouse and mice. Goose and geese. You are performing i-mutation — the ancient sound law that pulled a vowel toward i when a vanished -i suffix once followed it. German kept the suffix AND the vowel change, written as the two dots called umlaut: Mann → Männer, Fuß → Füße, Maus → Mäuse, Tochter → Töchter. English kept the vowel change and lost the dots. Your plurals are not a foreign system — they are your own fossil, still living on the continent.

footnotes.title: The Vanished Suffix
footnotes.content: Proto-Germanic plurals once ended in -iz for some nouns. The i pulled the root vowel forward (a→ä, u→ü, ou→eu), then the suffix itself wore away. German writes the pulled vowel with ä/ö/ü; English just kept the pulled vowel — man/men, foot/feet — with no spelling to explain it.

pattern.title: Five Plural Patterns, One Mutation Star
pattern.content: Pattern one, -er with umlaut: Mann → Männer, das Kind → die Kinder (no umlaut — the vowel never had an i to fear), das Buch → die Bücher (umlaut!). Pattern two, umlaut alone or with -e: der Apfel → die Äpfel, der Garten → die Gärten. Pattern three, -n/-en for the feminine squad: die Frau → die Frauen, die Zeit → die Zeiten, die Tochter → die Töchter (umlaut + n). Pattern four, -s for foreign and snappy words: das Auto → die Autos. Pattern five, no change at all: der Fernseher → die Fernseher — the -er agent nouns just stay. The dots are your friends: wherever German writes ä/ö/ü in a plural, English almost always changed the vowel too — Fuß/Füße ↔ foot/feet, Maus/Mäuse ↔ mouse/mice.
pattern.trap_note: Your mind will offer: “plurals add -e or -er.” German has several plural routes and no shortcut, but the article gives it away every time: die is plural as well as feminine. If you see die where you expected der, you are looking at a plural noun, not a feminine one.
pattern.linguist_note: Umlaut is a sound law, not a decoration: it applies whenever a historical i/j followed the root vowel — plurals (Mann/Männer), comparatives (kalt/kälter, next lesson), and verb mutations (geben/gibt — the same law you met in the strong verbs).

exercises.prompt: Match each singular with its umlaut plural — and its English fossil. Then recall earlier vocabulary in the short phrases:
exercises.target_answer: Männer, Füße, Töchter, Bücher, Blätter, Berge, Die Rechnung für die Bluse, die Lampe, ein Blatt, ein Ei, ein Knie
exercises.meaning: Mann → ? (man/men); Fuß → ? (foot/feet); Tochter → ? (daughter/daughters); das Buch → ?; Blatt → ? (leaf/leaves — the blade twin); Berg → ? (mountain, no dots needed); the bill for the blouse; the lamp; a leaf; an egg; a knee
exercises.explanation: The two dots mark the same vowel-pull English performed silently in men, feet, and geese — Blätter pulls them too; Berge takes the plain -e.

exercises.prompt: Which old connection is the odd one out in this set?
exercises.meaning: Recognize a familiar German word by choosing between earlier connection patterns.
exercises.explanation: Make, week and book use K → CH. Garden → Garten uses D → T.

exercises.prompt: Which plural takes the -s pattern (foreign and snappy words)?
exercises.explanation: Native nouns take -er/-e/-n or umlaut; the -s is the modern import lane — Autos, Fotos, Restaurants. The feminine -n squad sweeps your shelf: die Zeitung, die Rechnung, die Blume, die Lampe, die Bluse — every one takes -n in the plural.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: die covers plural as well as feminine
groß takes -e before a plural noun
exercises.explanation: Mann → Männer with an umlaut, Fuß → Füße the same way. The umlaut is the plural's vowel signal, and die is plural as well as feminine.
exercises.affirmation: You heard both umlauts and wrote them from memory of the law — ä and ü in the right places.

exercises.idea: you're sketching the beer garden for a friend: the men drink beer and the women drink tea
cues: Two umlaut plurals carry it: Mann → die Männer (man → men), Frau → die Frauen — then the plural verb trinken for both
exercises.target_answer: Die Männer trinken Bier und die Frauen trinken Tee
exercises.meaning: The men drink beer and the women drink tea

vocab_hints.note: das Bier — a mass noun here, no plural marker

exercises.explanation: Two umlaut plurals (Männer, Frauen) in one sentence — the fossil pair in the wild, built from a thought.

summary.outcome: Build umlaut plurals and sort nouns into the five plural patterns.

use_example.german: Die Männer trinken Bier und die Frauen trinken Tee.
use_example.english: The men drink beer and the women drink tea.

summary.takeaway: Umlaut is English's own fossil — Mann/Männer ↔ man/men — and five patterns cover the plural system.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the fossil umlauts — man/men and foot/feet prove i-mutation is your own buried treasure.

twist.prompt: Shrink the party: the men drink beer becomes THE MAN drinks beer. (Umlaut off, ending changes.)
twist.explanation: die Männer → der Mann: the umlaut plural dissolves back to singular, and the verb returns to the er/sie -t form. The umlaut is the plural's signature — remove it and the ending steps in.

mann.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *mann- — the identical twin of man; German keeps the short a English lengthened. [wiktionary]

frau.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *frawjǭ 'lady, mistress' — kin to archaic English frow 'lady'; Fräulein andMs.-style Frauennamen carry the same root. [wiktionary]

kind.context_translation: The child plays in the garden.
kind.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kindą, related to the root of English kin — 'of the family'. The t → z shift never fired here; the d hardened to t instead. [wiktionary]

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

buch.context_translation: I am reading a good book.

tochter.context_phrase: Meine Tochter lernt in der Schule.
tochter.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and gh → ch.

blatt.context_translation: The leaf falls from the tree.
blatt.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *bladą 'leaf' — English blade is the same word, meanings split. [wiktionary]

ei.context_phrase: Ich esse ein Ei zum Frühstück.
ei.context_translation: I eat an egg for breakfast.
ei.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *aij — Wiktionary lists English ey and egg as cognates. [wiktionary]

knie.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *knewą — the identical twin of English knee (silent k in both). [wiktionary]

zeitung.context_phrase: Er liest jeden Morgen die Zeitung.
zeitung.context_translation: He reads the newspaper every morning.
zeitung.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *tidungu, a message on the time-root — the page lists English tiding as the cognate: a Zeitung brings your tidings. [wiktionary]

berg.context_phrase: Der Berg ist im Winter weiß.
berg.context_translation: The mountain is white in winter.
berg.etymology_derivation: From Old High German bërg, from Proto-West Germanic *berg, from Proto-Germanic *bergaz. English barrow, a burial hill, is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

rechnung.etymology_derivation: rechnen + -ung — the twin of English reckoning; the entry lists English reckoning as a cognate. [wiktionary]

blume.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *blōmō 'blossom'; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

lampe.context_phrase: Die Lampe steht auf dem Tisch.
lampe.context_translation: The lamp is on the table.
lampe.etymology_derivation: From Latin lampada — the same Latin loan as English lamp. [wiktionary]

bluse.context_phrase: Die Bluse ist weiß und die Hose ist schwarz.
bluse.context_translation: The blouse is white and the trousers are black.
bluse.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French blouse - the same French word that gave English blouse. [wiktionary]
